title: To contemplate and hand on (ST II-II.188.6)
hook: better to light others than only to shine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adoro te devote, the hymn tradition gives to Thomas, adoring a God hidden under bread. Your line was godhead here in hiding.

A friend finishes a book that changed something in them, and for a week your phone keeps buzzing. A photo of a page. A line underlined twice. "You have to read this." Whatever lit them up, they can't keep it to themselves. Thomas Aquinas asked a question that sounds dry and isn't: which is the better life, one spent quietly gazing at God, or one spent busy doing good? His answer was neither, exactly.
screen: `YOU HAVE TO READ THIS.` → `GAZING, OR DOING?` → `THOMAS SAYS: NEITHER, EXACTLY.`

segments.voice: The question sits near the end of the long second part of the Summa, where Thomas weighs different ways of religious life. Some communities mostly pray, in silence. Some mostly serve: nursing, feeding, building. Thomas says contemplation, looking at God in prayer, is the higher thing in itself. But he puts a third kind of life highest of all: contemplating, and then handing on to others what you've seen. Teaching. Preaching. His picture is a lamp. It's a greater thing to give light than only to shine. A lamp glowing in an empty room is lovely; a lamp that lets someone find the door does more. The Latin phrase that comes out of this article is contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on to others what you've contemplated. Tradition says Thomas's own order, the Dominicans, took it as a motto. Notice the order: first you look, then you give. Thomas isn't praising busy people who never stop to pray, or people who only talk. The handing on has to come out of real looking, or there's nothing to hand on. Elsewhere in the Summa he points to the life of Jesus himself, who taught out of his own prayer. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works." One honest note: this is Thomas's argument, and the Church holds all these callings dear. Enclosed nuns who pray for the world, and sisters who run a hospital, aren't failing a test. Thomas is describing the shape of a gift: what you receive in silence grows when it's given away.
screen: `WHICH LIFE IS BETTER?` · `LOOK, THEN GIVE.` · `TO LIGHT, NOT ONLY TO SHINE.` · `ALL THESE CALLINGS ARE DEAR.` · then, large: `SO LET YOUR LIGHT SHINE BEFORE MEN.`

segments.voice: Look back over what you've learned lately, from this path, a book, a hard week, someone older, and let one thing rise that actually helped you: not the cleverest thing, the truest. Hold it a moment, the way Thomas would, just looking at it, then picture one person who could use it. If you pray, ask for the right moment to pass it on.
To contemplate and hand on. For Thomas, a life that looks at God and then gives others what it has seen, a lamp that lights the room, not only itself. Today's word.
screen: `TO CONTEMPLATE AND HAND ON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: light others. A lamp does the most when someone finds the door by it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Dominicans describe their life with the phrase contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on what has been contemplated, and Catholics draw on Thomas's article when they speak about prayer feeding teaching and preaching.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: contemplative life higher than active in itself (II-II.182.1); in 188.6 the life that teaches and preaches from the fullness of contemplation is ranked above the purely contemplative ('maius est illuminare quam lucere solum, ita maius est contemplata aliis tradere quam solum contemplari').
The claim that 'contemplata aliis tradere' became a Dominican motto is widely stated but not in the cited text; Keeper to confirm the wording 'became a motto of Thomas's own order'.
Jesus praying on the mountain and then teaching is given as Thomas's own appeal to Christ's example (188.6 and III.40.1 ad 2); confirm the attribution or soften.
'The Church holds all these callings dear' is added so the article's ranking of orders doesn't read as dismissing enclosed contemplative communities; confirm tone.

Editor pass: the Dominican-motto claim (not in the cited text) is now framed as 'tradition says'; the uncited 'prayed on the mountain, then came down to teach' appeal is replaced by a softer pointer to Christ's life, cited to III q. 40 a. 1 ad 2; howItsDone softened from 'often'.
